Treating each module as a bounded context, Catalog is upstream and Ordering downstream: when Catalog's contract changes, Ordering adapts; Catalog does not adapt to Ordering. CatalogProductPrices is a small anti-corruption layer translating int/CatalogProduct into Vnd.

claims.text: When two modules depend on each other, a change to either contract can break the other and neither can move out of the process alone; a cycle suggests the boundary is misplaced. Counting orders per product is about orders, so it belongs in Ordering.

Using ICatalog directly in Ordering's core would add a Domain-to-Catalog reference, spread Catalog's types into OrderService and need a stand-in for all of ICatalog in core tests; a port with one method avoids that.

A port and adapter between modules pay when the two models differ (int vs Vnd): a Catalog contract change or a move to another process changes only the adapter; if Ordering used Catalog's types unchanged, the adapter would translate nothing.
In an SDK-style .NET project, code can use another project's types only when that project is referenced in its .csproj via ProjectReference, directly or transitively through a referenced project.
